content.text: TypeScript lets you write the database layer, the API and the UI in one language, but it doesn't make them one skill. The server owns data, concurrency and security; the browser owns rendering, state and accessibility. This roadmap takes you from zero to senior in five stages: what to learn, what to postpone, one project per stage and the books worth your time.

A frontend developer who knows React well picks up a backend ticket: let users transfer credits to each other. Same language, same shared types, so the endpoint is done in an afternoon. The review comes back with three questions. What happens when two transfers from the same account arrive at the same moment? What stops a user from sending credits out of someone else's account? Why does the handler load every user into memory to find one? None of them is a TypeScript question.

The belief: one language from end to end means the backend and the frontend are the same skill, so learning one side teaches you the other. If you know TypeScript and React, a Node.js API is just more TypeScript.

It's easy to see why. The syntax is the same, npm is the same, and one type can describe a request body in both the form and the handler. Next.js puts server code and components in the same project, and the Node.js docs themselves call this a real advantage.

The same page also says that building apps for the browser is completely different from building a Node.js application. The browser gives you the DOM and web APIs; Node.js gives you the file system and the network, with no

. You choose the Node.js version on your server, never your visitor's browser. The language carries over; the problems don't. The server brings transactions, indexes, authorization and many users at once; the browser brings rendering, state, accessibility and slow phones.
What a full-stack TypeScript developer really does

A typical feature crosses the whole stack: design the tables and write a migration, add an endpoint with validation and authorization, build the page with its loading and error states, test both sides and ship. Between features you review pull requests, chase a slow query or a slow page, and update dependencies.
Shared types are the real win, and they hide a trap. Types don't exist at runtime: Node.js
runs TypeScript by stripping the annotations
and doesn't type-check anything. A handler whose body is typed as
receives whatever the client sent, so the server must still validate every input.
One language also hurts in specific places. CPU-heavy work, such as resizing images or parsing huge files,

that runs your JavaScript and freezes the whole server. Passing database types straight into the UI couples every page to your schema. And because both sides look alike, it's easy to lose track of which code runs where.

content.text: TypeScript checks your code, not your users' requests. Node.js strips the types and runs plain JavaScript, so a body declared as
can hold anything. Validate every input on the server with a runtime schema, and enforce authorization there even when the UI hides the button.

blocks.title: Grow one project through all five stages

content.text: Build one app, such as the expense tracker that becomes a booking system, and extend it at every stage instead of restarting from a fresh tutorial. You'll meet migrations, refactoring and your own old decisions, which is most of the real job.

Keep the project in one public repository with a README that says what it does and how to run it with one command. Let CI run the type check, the linter and the tests on every push, and keep a live demo deployed. Add two short write-ups: a bug that took you a day to find, and a trade-off you made, such as raw SQL over the ORM for one query. They say more about you than any list of technologies.
